To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) we propose a novel fixed reward function, which we call the evolutionary reward, (ii) we propose a way of approximating the joint action value, and (iii) we show that our technique outperforms CMA-ES in producing agents that maximizes the number of its own genes across time

we propose a fixed reward function that aims to maximize the number of current and future genetically similar agents and show that this reward function outperforms CMA-ES in producing agents that maximize the number of its own genes in two bio-inspired open-ended environments.
we introduce a new evolutionary reward function that is able to drive agents to maximise their reproductive success and we demonstrate its superiority to state-of-the-art techniques.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the optimisation of a fixed reward function that aims to maximize the number of current and future genetically similar agents.
the development of a new evolutionary reward, which is computationally inexpensive and produces agents that maximise their reproductive success.
the evolution of learning and the learning of evolution.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
our evolutionary reward function is a viable alternative to the state-of-the- art evolutionary algorithm, CMA-ES.

the evolutionary reward is an effective and viable alternative to the computationally intense optimisation of the agent’s reward function, and that it can be applied to a variety of bio-inspired environments.
our technique is a viable alternative to optimising the reward function in open-ended evolution, and it can be used in any evolutionary setting where the environment is not too complex.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
by mimicking evolution, we can learn to learn.
by using our evolutionary reward we can produce agents that are more genetically fit, and therefore more likely to be selected in future generations.

our proposed evolutionary reward, in conjunction with a genetic similarity weighted joint action value, can be used as a fixed reward function for open-ended environments, where the aim is to maximise reproductive success and survival.
The main takeaway from our work is that
by mimicking evolution, agents can learn better policies, and that by mimicking learning, evolution can better define the reward function.
we can mimic the evolutionary process in an efficient way, and in doing so, we can learn more about the evolutionary process itself.
we can use the evolutionary process itself to drive the evolution of agents.
